evidence: Source batches (source-1/2/3) maintained DO2 ~9–10 mg/L over 48–52 h, showing the receiving oxygen collapse is process-specific (estimated transfer multiplier 0.434, change ~48 h)
Delayed product assays (receiving): P(12h)=0.06, P(24h)=0.0, P(36h)=1.03, P(48h)=3.04 g/L — substantial accumulated product argues against stop

Forward model comparison at 52 h: strong_feed_reduction min DO 1.13 mg/L, oxygen deficit 4.32 mg·h/L, product mass 172.3 kg vs keep (1.01, 5.42, 171.3), increase_air (0.87, 8.67, 171.3), combined (0.96, 6.88, 171.4), reduce_feed (0.85, 8.67, 171.3)
args.rationale: Receiving DO2 collapsed at t≈48 h from ~10.7 to ~1.6–2.9 mg/L, at/below the 2.0 mg/L limit, while source batches sustained ~9–10 mg/L — indicating a receiving-specific oxygen-transfer deficit (model-estimated multiplier ~0.43). Air increase alone is insufficient (model: min DO 0.87, largest deficit). The strongest bounded feed reduction (0.6 feed + 1.15 air) minimizes oxygen demand and deficit (4.32 vs 5.42 keep), yields the highest predicted product mass (172.3 kg), and avoids a stop, which would zero counted production.
args.uncertainty: The forward model is source-calibrated and imperfect; across its sensitivity members no action achieves full feasibility (min DO 0.73–1.72 for strong_feed_reduction), so the improvement is partial. Timing of collapse and assay lag (4 h) limit knowledge of current product trajectory; feed reduction may somewhat slow further product accumulation versus keep.
